title: The Bitter Lesson
summary: Looking back over decades of AI research, the piece argues that general methods which scale with computation, namely search and learning, have always eventually beaten approaches that build in human knowledge, and that researchers should build meta-methods that discover rather than encode what we think we know.

title: Current AIs out-persuade professionals in lab settings but (probably) not in the world
summary: The author argues that experiments show AIs beating professional humans at narrow persuasion tasks, but real-world evidence suggests broad AI persuasion sits between median human and median professional level.

title: Can AI automate AI R&D yet?
summary: Using an evaluation called InnovationEval, the piece tests whether frontier AI models can independently rediscover a recent machine learning innovation, and finds they fall far short, reaching at most fifteen percent of the original gains while overstating their results. Progress is fast, so the authors plan to repeat the test on newer models.

title: Our AI Midwife
summary: A father describes how a chatbot playing a TV doctor suggested the MRI that found a fibroid behind his wife's six years of unexplained infertility, leading to a natural pregnancy after surgery. He uses the story to argue that AI's everyday benefits deserve acknowledgment alongside its risks.

title: Your Book Review: Storm Of Steel
summary: The reviewer argues that Ernst Jünger's Storm of Steel is the best war novel ever written, because it reports the First World War without a thesis. He links its theme of death and duty to his own ordeal when his daughter was born at twenty-four weeks.

title: Your Book Review: We Present Television
summary: A reviewer reads a 1940 collection of essays by the pioneers of American television, and finds it mostly prosaic technical description laced with startlingly accurate, and sometimes eerie, prophecy about the world television would build. The reviewer argues that "Television" meant far more than the TV set, and that its authors foresaw much of our connected, screen-saturated present.

title: James Bond: Jack Lowden and Callum Turner to screen test this weekend, reports say
summary: Reports say three to five actors, reportedly including Jack Lowden, Callum Turner and Josh O'Connor, are in the final screen tests to replace Daniel Craig as James Bond, with no timeline yet for a decision.

title: Andy Burnham defends Gogglebox appearance after Badenoch criticism
summary: Prime Minister Andy Burnham defended appearing on a celebrity Gogglebox episode for Stand Up To Cancer after Kemi Badenoch said she was amazed he had the time. Badenoch argued that a prime minister should be focused on the job rather than Gogglebox and social media.

title: We tried to automate Epoch
summary: Epoch tested leading AI models on its own regular work tasks, graded against the standards applied to human employees, and found the best scored about sixty-five percent, which is still a failing grade. This helps explain why AI's economic impact lags behind its benchmark results.

title: A World Driven By Fear
summary: Steve Magness argues that a media and political environment built on fear and outrage pushes society into a rigid, protective survival mode and trains helplessness, and that we can counter it by deliberately building hope through small, repeated actions.

title: Single points of failure in military AI command
summary: As autonomous systems replace human soldiers and officers, control of a military can collapse toward a single point of failure at the top. Nuclear command-and-control offers three kinds of safeguards, integrity, containment and soundness of command, but the ones that constrain the top are the least likely to be adopted.

title: What’s IN & what’s OUT in bi dating right now 👀
summary: Florence Scordoulis lists seventeen things that should be in and out of bi plus dating for cuffing season, from biphobic assumptions and app algorithms to queer belonging and timelines, while promoting a London bi plus speed dating and karaoke event.

title: We need more bees, so is honey the answer?
summary: The piece argues that beekeeping and eating honey do not help bee conservation, because managed western honeybees compete with, spread disease to, and pollinate less effectively than wild pollinators, and it urges better use of outdoor spaces and a plant-based diet instead.

title: ChinAI #379: “Chinese AI only makes trash TV?”
summary: Jeff Ding's newsletter examines a viral Chinese claim that over half of China's computing power goes to trash short dramas, traces it to a single investor statement, and notes a Banyuetan commentary debunking it. It also flags three further readings on recursive self-improvement, the global AI talent race, and past issues.

title: Evaluating how AI agents use tools
summary: AgentMail tested twenty-five model-and-harness agents on seven email tasks and found that agents rarely fail at the work itself, but at points where the tool leaves them guessing, such as hidden filtered mail, misleadingly named endpoints, and ambiguous spam labels. Most fixes belong to the tool: say what was filtered, name operations for what they do, and explain what labels mean.

title: Bruna's Marathon Comeback: From The Trails To The Roads for a 10-minute Personal Best
summary: Coach Marco describes how Bruna Maia returned from stress fractures to run a ten-minute marathon personal best in Chicago. He covers moving their coaching to the augo platform, her lab-tested physiology, and the training that fit her strengths.

title: Your Book Review: The Ghost In My Brain
summary: A reviewer who has her own concussion reads Clark Elliott's memoir of a decade of severe post-concussion symptoms and his recovery through puzzles and prism lenses. She weighs the thin evidence for the treatments and argues that patient communities, paired with structured case registries, could help decide what deserves a proper trial.

title: What's the ROI of software engineers' spending on AI?
summary: The author surveyed engineering leaders at twenty-seven companies, plus data from CodeRabbit and Gitar, to see what companies spend on AI per engineer and how pull request throughput changed. Spending varies widely and is unrelated to company size, and gains in throughput are uneven, with return on investment hard to pin down.

title: Jack Grealish: What next for England winger after 'breach of club discipline'?
summary: Everton left Jack Grealish out of their League Cup win over Newcastle because of a breach of club discipline, understood to be an unauthorised absence from training, raising questions about his future at the club.

title: How talking about Man Utd's cycle of doom became an industry
summary: The piece examines how constant commentary from former Manchester United players on podcasts and YouTube has turned the club's struggles into a content industry, and whether that coverage helps or harms the club.

title: Neural Networks Are Already Clean
summary: Nick Cammarata argues that apparent polysemanticity in neural networks is mostly recursive generalization rather than superposition, so a network's own neurons and circuits can be studied directly. He supports this with vision and language model experiments and argues for exploratory, agent-driven interpretability.

title: Against SURA
summary: The text supplied contains only the page header for this LessWrong post by Scott Alexander, with no article body, so the argument itself is not available.

title: Jack Grealish: What next for England winger after 'breach of club discipline'?
summary: Everton left Jack Grealish out of their League Cup win over Newcastle for a breach of club discipline, understood to be an unauthorised absence from training. The piece looks at what this means for the loan winger, whose mood and standing at the club appear to have shifted.

title: My California Ballot, 2026
summary: Scott Alexander walks through how he is voting in Oakland, California, on state propositions, state officials, local measures and local races, with his reasoning on each. He ends by testing whether an AI could have predicted his votes, and finds it only got fifty-seven percent right.

title: The Coverup Beneath the AI Hacking Scandals — Effort
summary: The piece argues that last quarter's AI cyberattacks stemmed from human error and nepotistic contracting among Effective Altruist organizations, not from rogue AI. It claims Anthropic and others should drop nepotistically hired contractors and employees.

title: vespers live artist/dj callout
summary: This is an application form inviting DJs, hybrid acts, and live electronic acts to apply to perform at Vespers Live, asking for contact details, sample work, social links, sound description, and availability.

title: America's Covid Fraud Totals Over $300B
summary: The author counts likely fraud across federal and state pandemic programs at over three hundred billion dollars, mostly in small business loans and unemployment benefits. The piece argues this follows from policy choices that skipped verification and rewarded spending over prevention, and that little has been recovered.

title: Effective Altruism is Buying Political Staff
summary: The piece argues that Open Philanthropy, now Coefficient Giving, and donors Dustin Moskovitz and Sam Bankman-Fried used political spending and fellowships to place hand-picked staff in US and UK government offices. It points to the UK AI Safety Institute, the Horizon Fellowship, and a Trump administration standards center as examples.

title: California's Race-Based Pregnancy Funding — Effort
summary: The piece argues that three California birth and motherhood programs restrict services by race while receiving federal Medicaid money, and that the Department of Justice could cut that funding under civil rights law.

title: AI Safety Donors Paid Religious NGOs $3.3M for Statements on AI
summary: The piece argues that AI Safety donors, chiefly the Future of Life Institute, have put about three point three million dollars into religious organizations since 2025 to produce public statements on AI, often without disclosure, and that this reflects a quasi-religious dimension of the AI safety movement itself.
